dossier.summary: The paper measures how accurately regression-based GATE estimators recover the global effect on an eight-case synthetic grid (SBM, BA and WS graphs at n=3000, five interference forms, Bernoulli and cluster assignment), scored on 24 fresh seeds by an evaluator built within the same project. Its headline numbers (frozen BIC-gated library 0.126 mean relative RMSE vs 0.180 for linear regression, 0.622 DiM, 0.994 HT, 0.045 oracle; coverage 0.839) all trace to the final evaluation run and match the delivered files. The paper is unusually candid about its limits: one graph size, one treatment probability, case specs shared with model selection, no ablation, no per-case intervals, and the mechanism account labelled a hypothesis. The selection-plane files and the record, however, show the library equal to plain linear regression in five or six of eight cases. Its plane-level gain comes almost entirely from case 6, whose exact generating sigmoid is in the library, and it is worse than linear in the count-by-degree case. That case's high error is therefore not evidence for the form-mismatch account. The study answers the task's question only partly: there is no analysis of bias versus variance or of how error scales, no design factor such as multiple treatment proportions, no public graph, and no flexible or GNN regressor on the final evaluation.

claims.quote: A frozen estimator that selects among 15 low-parameter exposure mappings with a BIC gate reaches a mean relative RMSE of 0.126, against 0.180 for plain linear exposure regression, 0.622 for difference-in-means, 0.994 for a neighbourhood Horvitz--Thompson estimator, and 0.045 for an oracle regression given the true mapping.

Per-case error is 0.031--0.054 in the five cases whose generating form is linear in the neighbour-treated fraction, across three graph families, a threefold change in interference strength and both assignment designs, and 0.151--0.452 in the saturating, count-by-degree and two-hop cases.

A BIC-gated library of parametric mappings lowered mean relative RMSE to 0.126 from 0.180 for plain linear regression, but remained 2.8 times above an oracle given the true mapping, did not fix the two-hop case, and produced intervals that cover only 0.839 of the time.

Relative RMSE was 0.031--0.054 per case in the five cases whose generating form is linear in the neighbour-treated fraction, regardless of graph family, a threefold increase in interference strength, or cluster versus Bernoulli assignment, and 0.198, 0.151 and 0.452 in the saturating, count-by-degree and two-hop cases.
scope_words: a threefold increase in interference strength

claims.quote: We hypothesize that exposure-mapping misspecification and corner extrapolation drive the larger errors, but the grid is not factorial and the estimator's per-case mapping choices were not verified, so this account is untested.
Nominal 95\% intervals cover only 0.839 of the time.
two other estimator classes (a flexible ridge ensemble and a linear model with a design-weighted residual correction) scored worse than the gated library on the model-selection seeds

These contrasts are consistent with the hypothesis that the mismatch between the generating form and a fraction-linear mapping, rather than graph family, strength or assignment, is what moves the error
the two-hop case stays at relative RMSE 0.452 and its cause is unresolved

issues.quote: In the three cases where the mechanism departs from that form it is 0.198 (saturating), 0.151 (count$\times$degree) and 0.452 (two-hop).
issues.why: On the model-selection seeds the plain fraction-linear regression has case-7 error 0.098 (estimator_02's metrics.json gives 0.0985, identical to the linear starter program in the record), close to cases 1 and 3, whereas the gated library has 0.183; the high count-by-degree error therefore comes from the studied estimator, not from a mismatch with a fraction-linear mapping, which undercuts the form-mismatch reading of the bimodal pattern.

issues.quote: A BIC-gated library of parametric mappings lowered mean relative RMSE to 0.126 from 0.180 for plain linear regression
issues.why: The delivered selection-plane metrics show the library's per-case errors equal to the linear-based estimator's to four decimals in cases 1, 3, 4, 5 and 8. It improves only case 6 (0.267 vs 0.708), whose exact generating sigmoid is in the library, and is worse in case 7. The plane-mean gain therefore reflects one case built into the library. The paper says only that the gain 'may partly' reflect this.

issues.quote: and the per-seed errors have a spread (Section~\ref{sec:reliability}) that is comparable to a fraction of it; we did not run a paired test.
issues.why: The headline frozen-vs-linear gap of 0.054 has no interval or paired test, and no dispersion is reported for the baseline values; the paper states this next to the claim.

issues.quote: We read single-factor contrasts as follows, each from one case pair, with the caveat that no per-case interval exists:
issues.why: Every factor contrast (e.g. 0.051 vs 0.031 for assignment design) is a single pair of per-case RMSEs with no interval, so 'no degradation' cannot be separated from seed noise; the paper concedes it.

issues.quote: We hypothesize that exposure-mapping misspecification and corner extrapolation drive the larger errors
issues.why: No experiment varies mapping fidelity or corner coverage at fixed graph and design, and corner coverage was not measured; the paper labels the account a hypothesis.

issues.quote: How Accurate Is Regression-Based Global Effect Estimation Under Network Interference? An Eight-Case Synthetic Evaluation
issues.why: The title and question are general, but the evidence is one studied estimator, one graph size (n=3000), one treatment probability (0.5), synthetic graphs only (no public graph, although the task asked for public graph data), and case specifications shared with model selection; the limitations section lists these.

issues.quote: the generating own-treatment effect also includes a treatment-by-covariate interaction that this regression omits.
issues.why: The linear baseline omits the treatment-by-covariate term that the generating model has and that the library's interaction mappings and the oracle include, and the HT reference is untuned; both are stated in the paper.

issues.quote: so we cannot report which mapping it selected in any case.
issues.why: The delivered selection-plane metrics show the library equal to the linear-based estimator in cases 1, 3, 4, 5 and 8 (two-hop 0.4453 in both), so it fell back to linear there; the two-hop mapping was never effectively used. A sentence saying so was removed from the draft, and the paper calls this 'not tested'.

issues.quote: Per-case bias is not recorded, so a substantial systematic component exists on average but is not shown to be concentrated in the cases with higher error.
issues.why: The task asks what determines the error. The paper gives only one plane-level bias figure (0.074, 0.588 of RMSE), with no per-case bias/variance split and no study of how the error scales with n. The evaluator, written in the same project, computes per-case bias but does not output it.

presentation.why: Main text cites internal file paths and function names (source_evidence/evaluator/evaluate.py, _linear_features, _ols_gate, candidate_designs, bic_gate, sandwich_se) instead of describing them.
Pipeline vocabulary ('final plane', 'outcome qualified', 'evaluator's declared requirements', 'evidence registry') shows how the study was produced and is not explained to the reader.

Terms such as 'plane', 'plane score' and 'frozen estimator' are used throughout without a clear definition. Many sentences are about missing records ('not recorded', 'not verified') rather than findings.
The overview schematic (Figure 1) packs three panels into the text width, so its labels and the case-grid table are too small to read in print.
Figure 3b is a single bar repeating two numbers already given in Table 2 (coverage 0.839, width 0.379), so it adds no information.

problems.why: No README or REPRODUCE file and no run commands. The only reproducibility notes are in the paper's appendix A.6.
The evaluators talk to the candidate through a broker proxy (/broker-code/candidate_proxy.py) and the pipeline's environment variables. Running them outside the original harness is undocumented.
The final-evaluation results directory is not delivered. The final per-case metrics and per-seed scores survive only as copies in paper/source/paper_data.json.
Per-case baseline errors, per-case bias and coverage, and the gate's chosen mapping per case are never written out, so the paper's per-case comparisons cannot be checked from the delivery.

process_notes: The same project wrote the evaluator, simulation grid and baselines in a task-drafting stage, with a calibration run of the baselines per case (task_drafting f1820a42 toolu_01KqDV6BhoxCdZ4bQgaTSKJd). That run already showed the linear regression's per-case search errors (case 6 0.708, case 7 0.098, case 8 0.445).

Three estimator classes were each evaluated once on the search plane; the first two failed the idea-level rubric. The first idea's plan (corner-coverage diagnostics, a public graph, 200+ replications per setting) was not carried out.

During writing, a figure comparing search-plane and final-plane per-case error, and a sentence saying the two-hop case stayed at 0.445 for the linear-based estimators and the library, were added and later removed.
No experiment was rerun after the paper first used the results; figures and derived statistics were regenerated from the same metrics several times.
fields.json: 5 of 38 agent invocations left no transcript, so some commands and edits are not visible.

integrity.why: The three estimator classes were compared and the library chosen on search seeds 101-108. The reported numbers come from one final run on seeds 9001-9024, whose graphs and assignments do not overlap with the search seeds. The case specifications are shared, which the paper states.

Evaluator, metric and case grid were built and fixed in the task-drafting stage, before any estimator existed. The edits to the evaluator template are transport and sandbox fixes. No edit of evaluate.py or the case specifications appears after the investigation began; the investigation's edits touch only the estimators' program.py.

The estimator sees only graph, covariates, assignment and outcomes. The investigation agents read search-plane aggregate and per-case metrics, but never the final-plane truth, the evaluator's mechanism code or the case-spec files. The library's exact case-6 sigmoid follows the qualitatively described grid, and the paper states this.

Every final-plane number traces to the final evaluation job via paper_data.json. Selection-plane numbers trace to the three search jobs, and derived statistics to build_figures.py runs; none was typed by hand.
